questions.corrige_markdown:
**Polymorphism** is the property of a substance of **existing in more than one crystalline form (different crystal structures) while keeping the same chemical composition**. The different forms are stable over different ranges of temperature and have different physical properties (shape, density, melting point) but the same chemical properties.

*Example:* sulphur exists as **rhombic sulphur** (stable below 96 $^\circ$C, octahedral crystals) and **monoclinic sulphur** (stable between 96 $^\circ$C and 119 $^\circ$C, needle-shaped crystals); both consist of $\mathrm{S_8}$ molecules and burn to give $\mathrm{SO_2}$. The temperature at which one form changes into the other (96 $^\circ$C) is called the **transition temperature**. For elements the phenomenon is also called **allotropy** (diamond and graphite, two forms of carbon); calcium carbonate is polymorphic (calcite and aragonite).

**Saponification** is the **alkaline hydrolysis of a fat or oil (an ester of glycerol and long-chain fatty acids) by boiling with a strong alkali**, such as sodium hydroxide, to give **glycerol and the sodium salt of the fatty acid, which is soap**.

$\text{fat or oil} + 3\mathrm{NaOH} \rightarrow \text{glycerol} + 3\ \text{sodium salt of fatty acid (soap)}$

In general: $\mathrm{C_3H_5(OOCR)_3} + 3\mathrm{NaOH} \rightarrow \mathrm{C_3H_5(OH)_3} + 3\mathrm{RCOONa}$

*In practice (soap making):* palm oil or another fat is boiled with sodium hydroxide solution; common salt is added to make the soap separate and float (salting out); it is then skimmed off, moulded and dried. With potassium hydroxide a soft soap is obtained. Soap is used for washing because one end of its ion dissolves in water and the other in grease.

**Isotopy** is the existence of **atoms of the same element with the same atomic number (same number of protons and electrons) but different mass numbers (different numbers of neutrons)**. These atoms are called **isotopes**. They have the same chemical properties (same electron arrangement) but slightly different physical properties (mass, density).

*Examples:* hydrogen has $^1_1\mathrm{H}$, $^2_1\mathrm{H}$ (deuterium) and $^3_1\mathrm{H}$ (tritium); chlorine has $^{35}\mathrm{Cl}$ (about 75 %) and $^{37}\mathrm{Cl}$ (about 25 %), which explains why its relative atomic mass is not a whole number:

$\dfrac{35 \times 75 + 37 \times 25}{100} = 35.5$

*Uses of radioactive isotopes:* carbon-14 for dating old objects, iodine-131 for the treatment of thyroid disorders, cobalt-60 for cancer treatment and sterilising equipment.

**Hydrolysis** is the **decomposition of a compound by water** (the compound is split into two or more products by reaction with water, often catalysed by an acid, an alkali or an enzyme).

*Examples:*

1. **Hydrolysis of an ester** (acid or alkali catalysed): $\mathrm{CH_3COOC_2H_5} + \mathrm{H_2O} \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{CH_3COOH} + \mathrm{C_2H_5OH}$ (with alkali the reaction is saponification).
2. **Hydrolysis of a salt of a weak acid** (the solution becomes alkaline): $\mathrm{CO_3^{2-}} + \mathrm{H_2O} \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{HCO_3^-} + \mathrm{OH^-}$, which is why sodium carbonate solution turns litmus blue.
3. **Hydrolysis of starch or sucrose** by dilute acid or enzymes into simple sugars (glucose); and of proteins into amino acids.
4. **Hydrolysis of anhydrous salts and of covalent chlorides**, for example $\mathrm{PCl_3} + 3\mathrm{H_2O} \rightarrow \mathrm{H_3PO_3} + 3\mathrm{HCl}$.
